title: The Queue Contract & FIFO Buffer Processing
summary: Understand the Queue interface: First-In-First-Out (FIFO) semantics, throwing vs special-value methods (add/offer, remove/poll, element/peek).
learningObjectives: Understand the formal First-In-First-Out (FIFO) contract of java.util.Queue
Master the dual method taxonomy: exception-throwing vs special-value return methods
Analyze bounded vs unbounded buffer constraints in producer-consumer pipelines
Implement asynchronous message processing buffers using Queue semantics
expectedOutcomes: Ability to select between add/offer, remove/poll, and element/peek based on failure mode requirements
Mastery of thread-safe pipeline design foundations using Queue primitives

activities.title: Practical Context: Airport Security Screening Checkpoint Lanes

analogy.headline: Practical Context: Airport Security Screening Checkpoint Lanes
analogy.story:
Imagine an airport security screening checkpoint lane. Passengers enter at the back of the stanchion lane (the tail) and wait their turn. The TSA officer at the front of the lane (the head) inspects one passenger at a time. The first person who stepped into the line is strictly the first person screened and cleared (First-In, First-Out).

If the waiting lane is cordoned off with a fixed physical capacity of 20 people (a bounded buffer), a newly arriving traveler cannot force their way in without the agent turning them away (offer returns false). If the line is completely empty, the agent simply rests and waits rather than triggering an emergency alarm (poll returns null).

This is precisely how the Java Queue interface models data flow.
analogy.keyTakeaway: Queues model FIFO sequencing where insertion occurs at the tail and extraction occurs at the head. Methods come in pairs: throwing exceptions or returning special values.

activities.title: The Queue Architecture: Dual Method Forms & FIFO Buffer Semantics

keyTakeaways: Queue models First-In-First-Out (FIFO) ordering where elements are added at tail and removed from head
Methods come in dual forms: Throwing exceptions (add, remove, element) vs Returning special values (offer, poll, peek)
In bounded buffers, offer() returns false on overflow; poll() returns null on underflow
Queue implementations generally disallow null elements because null is used as a sentinel return value by poll() and peek()

activities.title: Bounded Message Processing Pipeline
activities.description: Trace a bounded telemetry message buffer that safely rejects overflow packets without throwing exceptions.

steps.description: Initialize a private Queue backed by ArrayDeque with an enforced integer capacity limit.
Check if buffer.size() >= maxCapacity before calling buffer.offer(packet). If full, return false cleanly without crashing.
Consume packets via buffer.poll(). Returns the head element in FIFO order or null if the queue is drained.

questions.question: What is the difference between queue.remove() and queue.poll() when called on an empty queue?
options: remove() throws a NoSuchElementException; poll() returns null
remove() blocks the thread; poll() throws an exception
remove() returns false; poll() returns true
questions.explanation: remove() is the exception-throwing form that throws NoSuchElementException on empty queues; poll() returns null to signal empty status gracefully.

questions.question: Why do standard Queue implementations strongly discourage or forbid inserting null elements?
options: Because poll() and peek() use null as a sentinel return value to indicate the queue is empty
Because Java arrays cannot hold null references
Because JVM garbage collection crashes on null in queues
questions.explanation: If null were stored in a queue, a caller receiving null from poll() could not distinguish between an empty queue and a queue whose head element is null.

questions.question: Which method is the special-value counterpart to queue.add(e) when inserting into a bounded queue that is full?
questions.explanation: While add(e) throws an IllegalStateException if a bounded queue is full, offer(e) returns false to indicate rejection.

questions.question: What order does a standard FIFO Queue guarantee when extracting elements?
options: First-In, First-Out: elements are extracted in the exact chronological sequence they were inserted
Random order based on memory address
questions.explanation: A standard FIFO queue guarantees that the earliest inserted element remaining in the buffer is always the first one extracted at the head.

questions.question: Why should high-throughput backend services prefer offer/poll/peek over add/remove/element in Queues?
questions.answer: In high-throughput services, queues routinely reach capacity or become empty during normal operation. Throwing exceptions (like IllegalStateException or NoSuchElementException) requires JVM stack trace construction and frame unwinding, which consumes significant CPU cycles and creates GC pressure. Special-value methods (offer returning false, poll returning null) execute in constant nanosecond time without allocating exception objects.

questions.question: How does java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue extend the java.util.Queue contract?
questions.answer: BlockingQueue adds blocking operations for producer-consumer multi-threading: `put(e)` blocks until space becomes available if the queue is full, and `take()` blocks until an element becomes available if the queue is empty. It also provides time-bounded overloads like `offer(e, timeout, unit)` and `poll(timeout, unit)`.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of add, poll, and peek in ArrayDeque and LinkedList?
questions.answer: Both ArrayDeque and LinkedList achieve O(1) time complexity for add, poll, and peek at the head and tail. However, ArrayDeque has a much lower constant factor: it uses a contiguous circular array with zero object allocations, whereas LinkedList allocates a 24-byte Node object on every insertion, incurring pointer dereferencing and memory fragmentation.

I understand why null elements are rejected by modern Queue implementations
I can implement FIFO producer-consumer buffers using ArrayDeque

practiceProblems.title: Drain Queue to List
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement drainQueue(Queue<String> queue) that polls elements one-by-one from the queue and returns them in a List in FIFO order until the queue is empty.

practiceProblems.title: Safe Peek with Fallback
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement inspectHead(Queue<String> queue, String fallback) returning the head element via peek() if present, or fallback if the queue is empty or null.
hints: Call queue.peek(). If null, return fallback.

practiceProblems.title: Batch Processing Queue
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement processBatch(Queue<Integer> queue, int batchSize) that polls up to batchSize items from the queue and returns their sum.

practiceProblems.title: Recent Event Buffer
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Implement a class RecentEventBuffer that holds at most N events. When a new event arrives and the buffer is full, remove the oldest event before adding the new one.
hints: If buffer.size() >= capacity, call buffer.poll() first.

practiceProblems.title: Count Elements Matching Condition Without Emptying Queue
practiceProblems.problemStatement: Given a Queue<Integer>, count how many elements are even numbers without permanently altering the queue contents or ordering.
hints: Poll each element, test condition, and offer it back to the tail.
Repeat exactly queue.size() times to restore original sequence.
